newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RUGBY UNION-A salute to Zinny on eve of his 50th test.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-A salute to Zinny on eve of his 50th test.

text.p: CHRISTCHURCH, July 3 - When Zinzan Brooke leads the All Blacks out at Lancaster Park on Saturday, his temporary leadership of the world's best rugby team will be more than just a tribute to his 50th test appearance, NZPA reports.
It will also recognise one of the world's greatest No 8s, test rugby's most skilful forward, and the player who has redefined back-row play in the recent years.
Description of the player has come in many ways -- from flamboyant, wonderfully skilled, aggressive defender, delightful attacker to total rugby player of the modern age.
Those words have nevertheless been apt for the range of skills this backrower displays.

If he was allowed, the 32-year-old Blues captain could adequately feed the scrums and then clear the ball with one of his spiralling passes, whether it's a diving one, back-handed flick or the conventional bullet-type.
He could even throw into the lineout or hook the scrum.
"There's nothing Zinzan can't do on the field," his Auckland and Blues coach Graham Henry says.
"I've learnt not to be surprised by his acts. He's not afraid of having a go, that's the confidence of the player."
Rugby fans don't have to have a good memory of Brooke's deeds, there is always a new one coming.
In the first test against Argentina at Athletic Park two weeks ago he drew the defence on the right and cross-kicked to his brother Robin who scored on the left.
While the all-purpose era has just dawned on rugby, Brooke has been a multi-dimensional player for years.
It comes, he said, naturally to him.
"You sort of don't think. A situation arises and you respond to it," he said.

Brooke is a fierce forward, gifted at grabbing at the opposition. He can range all over the field in attack or defence, he flicks out deft passes, he's an unerring decision-maker. A born leader even though he is not the All Blacks captain.
He scores tries down the wing, behind the scrum and drops improbable goals from long distances.
Some coaches might deem Brooke too much of a maverick to hold up as a role model for the modern test forward.
But the modern game calls for multi-talented men with a maverick trait -- a trait alien to generations of All Black forwards who have gone before him.
His captain, Sean Fitzpatrick, confesses to alarm whenever Brooke grabs the ball.
"You tend to say 'hang on, let's decide what's best from here' on the field but by then Zinzan's gone -- the decision's made, the move's been executed and five points are on the board."
The "new South Africa" test at Ellis Park in 1992 was a classic case of Fitzpatrick's dilemma.
A penalty inside the Springboks' 22 in the dying minutes came New Zealand's way. Every one of the 80,000 crowd expected Grant Fox to kick for goal and Fitzpatrick would have made the same decision.
The trouble was he never came around to making the call.
Brooke ordered the ball from Michael Jones, tapped, raced and smashed through for the decisive try. New Zealand won the test 27-24. It was one of Brooke's most memorable moments in the sport.
The response from Fitzpatrick was: "What the hell did you do that for? But..."

"I never realised I did it. I saw the Springboks tighties (tight forwards) -- three or four of them -- with their backs to me. I was sure they were thinking that Foxy was going to kick for goal and it was that moment I thought tap and go," Brooke said.
Ironically, Brooke wasn't going to be on that tour as he had just returned from playing in Italy.
"That was the turning point of my career," he said.

Brooke started as midweek captain, playing blindside flanker on the '93 tour of Britain. He was switched to the openside and scored four tries in the match against South of Scotland, winning the No 7 jersey for the tests against Scotland and England.
Under Laurie Mains, Brooke's selection was a hit and miss situation where Aaran Pene and Mike Brewer were rivals.
But with the appointment of John Hart, Brooke, along with others, thrived through the greater liberty presented by the coach, allowing them to express their skills.
The first real test of that came in last year's Bledisloe Cup at Athletic Park.
A magnificent All Black team played almost flawless rugby in what for ordinary mortals should have been impossible conditions, Wallaby coach Greg Smith said.
Mud being a great leveller is an old rugby adage. But not for the All Blacks that day, they won 43-6 and Brooke capped yet another memorable game.
That Athletic Park match and the 1995 World Cup semifinal win against England, where Brooke potted a "ripper" drop goal before 40 million television viewers, stand out most for Brooke.
However, there are other moments that remain picture-like in Brooke's mind.
In 1992, while he and brother Robin were playing the off-season in Italy, the phone rang one evening.
"I answered the phone and the voice said, 'it's Laurie (Mains), can I speak to Robin?'
"I said 'it's Zinzan here'.
"The answer was 'yeah, I want to speak to Rob'," Brooke recalled with a laugh.
"Robin got on the phone and blah, blah, blah. Laurie wanted Robin back in New Zealand for the trials.
"I said, 'hold on a sec'. And when Robin jumped on the plane I was right there behind him."
In 1990, the All Blacks toured France with Alex Wyllie was coach. The test No 8 spot was open.
"Grizz (Wyllie) never picked his No 8 that day. It was in a training session and Mike Brewer just came and slotted himself in the spot and then he just ran onto the field for the test," Brooke said.
"Seven years on Mike and I still laugh about it. The No 8 was never picked."
The axing of Wayne "Buck" Shelford as No 8 and All Black captain in 1990 shook Brooke, who was the replacement.
"It was like a New Zealand son had been killed," Brooke recalled to the reaction from rugby followers.
"No matter how I played that day there was always going to be that disappointment about Buck being dropped for reasons I don't know.

"I probably took a lot on myself thinking that I just had to prove it to the people. I thought I just have to perform for New Zealand but I should have thought I should do it for myself. I don't think I played that well."
Brooke's 10-year test span starting with the 1987 World Cup has yielded just 50 tests. Injuries like the infamous "eggs on my leg" injuries preceding the '95 World Cup restricted his career.
Nevertheless, he's peerless for what he's provided on the rugby field.
"I feel really privileged to play the 50th (91st match in all)," Brooke said.
"But I don't look at records anymore. A few years ago a I used to hunt them out."

He has scored 177 points in the All Black jersey from 39 tries and two drop goals, including 15 test tries. Now he has a New Zealand Rugby Union contract secured until just before the 1999 World Cup and there's bound to be more Zinzan magic on the field preceding that.
